speechtext:

2.	Is it the government's intention to close all hospitals situated on the reserves and in particular "the reserves situated at Morley and Gleichen, Alberta?

speakeroldname: Mr. Hubert Badanai (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: INDIAN CLAIMS COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am informed by the Departments of Citizenship and Immigration and National Health and Welfare as follows:
1.	Proposed Indian claims legislation was submitted to all Indian bands and Indian organizations for study on August 7. The representations have been reviewed and a bill with certain modifications will be available shortly for consideration as the business of the house may permit.
[Mr. Lamontagne.l
2.	Departmental experience has been that small hospitals situated on Indian reserves do not provide economic or efficient hospital service to the native population. For this reason it has been longstanding policy to close such hospitals whenever adequate community facilities become available.
The departmental facility on the Morley Indian reserve has never been recognized as a hospital by the provincial hospital authority. Its primary function is that of providing a base for the two nurses engaged in the public health program on the reserve and clinic accommodation for visiting medical and dental staff. There are also several beds in reserve for the emergent care of patients who cannot be moved to conventional community hospitals.
The department does not intend to close out the Blackfoot Indian hospital at Gleichen, Alberta, until adequate alternative facilities are available in the community.

subtopic: CRASH POSITION INDICATOR
CRASH POSITION INDICATOR
speechtext:
1.	Does a company called Leigh Instruments produce a crash position indicator commonly called the beacon, foUowing a project and research developed by the national research council and, if
Questions
so, what are the details in brief of this instrument, according to national research council authorities?
2.	Is this instrument used on R.C.A.F. planes?
3.	Is this instrument used on Air Canada and/or C.P.A. planes?
4.	Has Air Canada any comparable kind of instrument and, if so (a) has it been fitted on any of the jet planes of Air Canada and (b) for what period of time?

subtopic: CRASH POSITION INDICATOR
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Defence Production, National Defence and Transport as follows:
1.	Yes. This device consists of a miniaturized battery powered radio beacon which is encapsulated in a foam plastic package installed near the rear of the aircraft. The package is relatively flat in shape so that it resembles an aerofoil. In the event of a crash, the crash position indicator is automatically released at the instant of impact. During the period of a few thousandths of a second in which the destruction of the aircraft is initiated, the crash position indicator is deployed away from the impact point by the aerodynamic forces associated with the velocity of impact and is decelerated to a safe landing speed.
The over-all dimensions of the crash position indicator are 20" X 20" X 4", and it weighs approximately six pounds. It produces a signal on a distress frequency for about three days, and this signal can be detected by search aircraft at ranges of between 20 and 40 miles.
When installed on a large aircraft, the crash position indicator is capable of surviving any likely crash circumstances. On small aircraft, its ability to survive is only limited at extremely adverse combinations of impact angle or speed.
2.	Yes, an accident data recorder-crash position indicator developed by Leigh Instruments is undergoing prototype evaluation in one Yukon aircraft.
3.	No.
4.	No.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS JURISDICTION RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg asked me a question concerning the date by which ownership of offshore mineral rights would be determined as between the federal and provincial governments.
At the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa on October 14, 1964, the question of jurisdiction as between the federal government and the provinces concerning offshore mineral rights was discussed. There was a wide difference of views on the legal rights of the different governments. Therefore on December 11, 1964 I wrote to each of the premiers and said that the diversity of views with respect to the questions involved confirmed the view of the federal government that it was essential to have an authoritative clarification of the legal position. This is 20220-732
Inquiries of the Ministry necessary in the national interest because of the need to encourage the exploration and development of these offshore resources which cannot be effectively developed while jurisdictional uncertainty continues.
I advised the premiers that the government had decided that the various aspects of the problem should therefore be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada. I expressed the hope that the provinces would join in the preparation of the reference to the Supreme Court of Canada so there could be an agreed basis if at all possible.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, the Department of Justice is preparing draft documents containing the terms of reference to the supreme court, and it is a very complicated reference indeed. These will be forwarded to the premiers for their comments at the earliest possible time.
It is not possible to give any certain date by which this matter will be determined, but I want to assure the hon. member that the federal government is anxious to have such a determination as expeditiously as possible.

subtopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN DEALING WITH AMENDMENT METHOD
speechtext:
I would like to reply to the question which the hon. member for Greenwood first addressed to me on November 6, 1964, and which he followed up on February 16, 1965, concerning the submission to parliament of the constitutional amendment procedure approved at the federal-provincial conference last October.
Since October I have written to the provincial premiers on two occasions about this matter. On November 3, 1964, I asked their concurrence in the accuracy of the final draft of the text of the proposed "Act to provide for the amendment in Canada of the constitution of Canada", including the schedule in which the act in its French version is reproduced. On January 5, 1965, I sent them a draft of a white paper on this subject and invited their comments on it. I should like now to table copies of my letters, together with copies of the written replies that have been received so far.
It will be seen from this exchange of correspondence, supplemented in certain cases by oral communications, that good progress is being made in the complex of decisions and actions which are required at both the provincial and federal levels before the agreed amending formula can be enacted into law. The government of Newfoundland has notified the government of Canada of its approval of the proposed act. The other provinces, in conveying their acceptance of the final text as being accurate, have indicated that they are considering the course they should follow to obtain the concurrence of their legislatures. Several governments have already placed a resolution for concurrence on the order papers of their legislative assemblies.
All the provinces have now agreed that the draft white paper on the "Amendment of the constitution of Canada", which is to be published by the federal government, satisfactorily sets forth the history of the efforts to achieve agreement on an amending formula as well as the nature and effects of the plan that has now been agreed on. The white paper is now being printed in both its English and French versions. The government will be able to table it in both houses of parliament next week. Copies will then be made available to provincial governments for distribution to members of their legislatures

and for other official provincial purposes. Copies will also be available for general distribution.
It is the intention of the government to submit the amendment procedure to parliament at the next session. The timing and procedure of parliamentary action must be co-ordinated with the requisite provincial action, and the government therefore is not yet in a position to suggest precisely what timing and procedure it will recommend to parliament in dealing with this matter.
In his supplementary question of February 16 the hon. member for Greenwood asked whether consideration was being given to enlarging the scope of parliamentary consideration of the amendment procedure to include the whole question of constitutional amendment. The government believes that it would be unwise at this time to link the question of the amending procedure to that of revision of the constitution. The enactment of the amending procedure will make our present constitution fully Canadian. That is the first thing to achieve. When we have achieved it then we can better go on to consider whether there are revisions in the constitution that Canadians as a whole may wish to make.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he has an answer to the question I posed to him on Thursday regarding the charge made by striking workers of Chrysler Canada Limited that under the new agreement between the United States and Canada, automobiles were being imported by that company duty free.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: I think my hon. friend the Minister of Industry is in a position to say something about that.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext:
There are two parts to the answer to this question. The first is that an inquiry has been made and it has been discovered that the Chrysler corporation is importing motor vehicles from the United States, on the bulk of which duty has been paid. They are not all entering duty free.
Second, under the terms of the new tariff item relating to this agreement it is not possible for a motor car manufacturer in Canada to import motor vehicles duty free from the United States, unless he continues to maintain a ratio of production in Canada to his domestic sales not lower than the base year 1964. It would not, therefore, be possible for the Chrysler corporation, under this agreement, to do what has been alleged, namely to import from the United States on a duty free basis rather than produce in Canada.

subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Will the minister give us an assurance now that the Chrysler corporation are not importing cars duty free during this period of time?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I cannot and will not give such an assurance. The agreement contemplates the right of the Chrysler corporation, along with other Canadian car manufacturers, to import duty free motor vehicles provided they meet certain tests. One of those tests is that their production in Canada, in relation to total sales, shall be not less than it was in the base year 1964. So long as the Chrysler corporation or any other corporation continues to maintain that ratio they have, and will continue to have, the right to import duty free.

subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: Will the minister explain to the house why this agreement can be put into effect without a reciprocal agreement by the congress of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext:
The agreement with the United States, Mr. Speaker, is an agreement by the administration of the United States to seek from the congress of the United States the retroactive removal of tariffs on automobiles and automobile parts entering the United States from Canada. The administration is now in the process of executing its part of that agreement, namely seeking congressional authority. In the case of Canada, in order to allow the substantial improvement made under the earlier incentive plan to continue

without interruption we have removed, for Canadian manufacturers of motor vehicles, the tariff on the entry of motor vehicles and motor vehicle parts.

subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question on this important matter. If the congress of the United States does not approve this agreement within the next six months, would not the minister think this would be a one way street under this agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: I am being asked for an opinion. The administration is seeking the removal of this tariff on the basis that its removal will be dated back to the signing of the agreement. If this is not done for six months but the removal is still dated back it will make no difference.

subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: In the event that the legislation passed by the United States is not back-dated to January 1, 1965, may I ask the minister if it is the government's intention to collect duties retroactively up to the time the United States removal date becomes effective?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext: May I ask the minister, then, is there any provision by which this agreement will be cancelled in the event the United States legislation does not conform with the original plan the two governments had in mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext:
There is provision in the agreement for both termination and a review. I do not believe this is exactly the right time to try to explain in detail what the agreement does contain. It is, in my view, a very advantageous agreement for both countries.
In reply to the particular question the hon. gentleman has asked, I may say it is a hypothetical one. However, it is extremely unlikely that the United States congress will not follow the recommendations of the administration in respect of the removal of the United States tariff.

subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE
speechtext:
I am sure the minister agrees that the questions indicate the great advantage it would be to the house if this resolution were introduced fairly early so the house could get the full information. May I ask the minister if we could have his assurance, in view of the strike situation, that the Chrysler Corporation will not be allowed to bring into Canada any larger percentage of their total sales for 1965 than was the case in 1964?
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: CHRYSLER CANADA LTD.-DUTY FREE IMPORT OF CARS WHILE EMPLOYEES ON STRIKE

While I am still on my feet, Mr. Speaker, may I also refer to a question asked me the other day by the hon. member for Shefford, which he believed was urgent. I would like to clarify the situation now.
There seems to have been considerable misunderstanding and misinterpretation of a comment I made on the subject of farm income during a news conference a few weeks ago, and perhaps I can clear it up at this time. During the debate on my department's estimates in October, 1963 the hon. member for Qu'Appelle presented a bunch of figures to illustrate what we already knew, that many of our farmers need a better living. The comment he made that stuck in my crop was a reference to a set of figures which he said indicated that 25 per cent of the farmers across Canada earned less than $1,200 from their farms.
At the news conference I was trying to make the point that I just could not accept these figures, whatever their source, as an accurate reference to the gross income of any Canadian farmer who can honestly call himself a farmer. I was not suggesting that $1,200 a year or $2,400 a year in gross income is anywhere near enough for any farmer to live on decently. I was only arguing that any farmer with two hogs and six cows had a potential gross income of more than $2,400 a year, whatever economists and politicians, more at home in ivory towers than in barnyards, might argue to the contrary.
I reasoned in this way. If a farmer has only two sows they would each have two litters of pigs a year, and if they just made the national average of eight pigs per litter that would come to 32 pigs in a year. If they were sold on the Montreal market when they were five or six months old and weighed about 200 pounds they would bring something like $40 apiece. That is a gross income of $1,280, and he still has the two sows.
If, in addition to the two sows, he has six cows each giving the national average of 8,000 pounds of milk per year, that is 48,000 pounds of milk. At the current Quebec price of $3.20 per cwt. that is a gross income of

$1,536, although figuring it in my head at the news conference I just used a round figure of "over $1,200." So if you add the hog gross of $1,280 to the milk gross of $1,536 you get a total gross income of $2,816 for a farmer with two sows and six cows.
My contention at the news conference was, and still is, that anybody who does not have a couple of pigs and half a dozen cows around his place just should not consider himself a farmer. That kind of rural dweller should not be included in statistics intended to give an accurate picture of our farm problems.

speechtext:
Before this clause carries I should like to make one or two comments concerning the bill. I think it is fair to remind

Canada Pension Plan
the committee that there has been an extensive study of this measure in committee. I believe some 51 meetings were held, in the course of which a great deal of evidence was heard and many briefs were presented. These have been helpful.
It can also be said with fairness, I think, that this is one of the most complex pieces of legislation ever to come before the house. It is also one of the most important pieces of legislation to come before us for consideration, inasmuch as it is bound to have long term effects on the future of Canada.
Before I continue with my general remarks, let me say this. I was under the impression at one stage, perhaps through inadvertence, that the resolution which the Prime Minister tabled on Wednesday or Thursday would probably be discussed first of all as we returned to this particular piece of legislation. I understand now that it is to be discussed when we reach part IV of the bill, the part which has to do with old age security.
I am taking it for granted that when part IV is reached and this resolution is discussed, it will pass the house. I do not think there is any doubt about that; I am taking it for granted. At the same time it is important that we should know just where this projected expenditure will take us. In the committee we were, it is true, given an actuarial report. In addition we were presented with an economic report in relation to the Canada pension plan. But I am suggesting now that the government should be prepared to make available an economic report on the effects these proposals will have on old age security benefits.
I am sure the department must have some figures on this already. Prior to the new resolution it had been suggested the amendments were to provide that old age security payments could be reduced to $51 a month and that other amounts would be reduced on an actuarial basis depending on the age at which a recipient or beneficiary wished to benefit. We would like very much to see a report showing the effects not only of the escalation which was in the bill prior to the recent resolution but also what the effect of the recent resolution will be on the old age security fund. I am referring to the escalation, the reduction of the qualifying age to 65, and the $75 pension. I make this request now to make sure that we may have an economic report before us by the time we discuss the resolution, when part IV is reached.
At the time the Prime Minister made his statement it was indicated in newspaper

clippings and so on-I did not see the actual press release, and I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman mentioned it in the house-that the additional cost might be in the neighbourhood of $180 million or $185 million by 1970. I refer to this now so that when we come to the resolution we shall have before us information showing exactly what this will mean to the old age security fund in the years to come.
I am sure all members of the committee will agree with me when I say this is one of the most complex pieces of legislation which has ever come before us. I believe that ample debate on this measure is called for, and in this connection I should like to quote briefly from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail on February 18:
The plan is of vital importance to every Canadian. Almost the entire house is in favour of it in principle, and every member has a duty to play his part in seeing that it is the best plan possible within our means. The real calamity would be if they did not.
If it takes time, well, important matters cannot be rushed, and surely on such an issue no government retaining its senses would consider closure.
I am simply putting forward the thought that this measure is of fundamental importance to the economy of Canada. We want to get the best out of it we possibly can for all people. I would refer briefly to one sentence in the minister's statement in the white paper, where she said:
This is to establish a contributory pension plan ensuring that as soon as possible in a fair and practical way all Canadians will be able to look forward to retiring in security and with dignity.
It was for this reason that the bill received such an enthusiastic reception on second reading and that it was endorsed in principle. But only after our long deliberations in the committee has it been possible to determine the weaknesses of the measure. I propose to ask some questions concerning these weaknesses.
I should like at this stage to return to item No. 8 of the third report of the joint committee which was tabled in this house on February 16. Appendix D which is attached thereto contains certain definite amendments, some important and some really only technical amendments-changes in wording and that sort of thing. Item No. 8 recommends, however, that consideration be given to many other suggestions, and I should like to point out that we have many ideas about ways in which this bill can be improved. When the appropriate time comes we intend to suggest amendments for the consideration of the

house. However, I should like to ask now whether the minister would table the amendments or give them to the committee orally so that there would be on the record some indication of the actual amendments that she is going to propose. I think this would be very helpful and would only lead to a proper discussion of the bill as we go through it clause by clause. I wonder whether the minister would consider that at this stage?
I do not see the minister voluntarily rising from her seat at the moment, Mr. Chairman, so I will continue.
I should like to point out that as of this morning, at least, the minutes of the final committee meeting had not arrived in my office, and I think that they should have been available to the house at large before we came back to committee stage. As we all know, only a certain number of members can sit on a committee, and only those members who attended fairly regularly and dutifully could be in a position to discuss the clauses with some knowledge, in view of the complexity of the bill, all the cross references to be made, and that sort of thing. However, I would come back to the point I was making, that I should like the government to give us an opportunity to see what amendments they are going to make.
The Prime Minister said either last Wednesday or Thursday that he had one further suggestion to make on top of several rather inconsequential amendments, I think he said. However, even though they be inconsequential I am sure it would be advantageous to a reasonable discussion of the bill if we had some idea in advance of what the government are proposing by way of amendments.
I am not going, Mr. Chairman, into the history of the Canada pension plan. However, I would point out in a very few words that it has had many alterations. I think it is sufficient to say that we are now on what I would call the sixth plan. Others would call it the fifth, and I am not going to quibble about whether it is the fifth, the sixth, the third or the fourth, but I do know that we have had many alterations to it. The latest was the proposal made by the Prime Minister the other day. However, I should like to mention what I feel, and what we as the official opposition feel, are very definite shortcomings in the plan, and at the appropriate time we will make some suggestions concerning them. We feel there are so many shortcomings that if we are going to make amendments to it, as we propose to do, it would be much more beneficial and save time
Canada Pension Plan
for us all if the government would see fit to present to us their amendments at this time.
There are, Mr. Chairman, two general questions I should like to ask. It was pointed out in the Ontario brief that the royal commission on taxation had been meeting for more than two years, and it was suggested that at least a preliminary opinion from that commission on the implications of the Canada pension plan as it affects the incidence of taxation should be obtained. This request was made on February 1, which I think is three weeks ago today, and I am wondering whether the royal commission on taxation has been asked for a preliminary opinion in order to ascertain what they feel about the impact of the Canada pension plan on the over-all taxation picture. I think this is even more important, now that the Prime Minister has made this further announcement, with which we all agree but which we believe should be set out in more detail.
One other question which I should like to put to the minister is this. Have there been any conversations or contacts with the Ontario government in order to discuss the possibility of meeting that government at least part way in their attempts to improve the present plan? We feel that the Ontario government submitted a very good, in fact excellent, brief. We feel that it goes a long way toward meeting the shortcomings which we feel are in the bill. While I do not say that these suggestions should be accepted in full, I do believe that this government should at least have some discussions with the Ontario government to see whether there is any meeting ground on which the two views could come together.
A third question which I might ask, and which I also think was suggested in the committee-I think the evidence would show that this question was asked of government members of the committee-is this. It was pointed out that originally the province of Quebec had asked for a 20 year transition period, as had the province of Ontario. It was suggested in the committee that it might be possible to discuss this further request from the province of Ontario with the province of Quebec. Quebec, having originally asked for this particular consideration in the plan, I should like to ask whether the government has at any stage since the committee, discussed this matter with the province of Quebec.
I should now like to return to my own ideas about this bill. I have one personal view as to one particular shortcoming. I must admit

Canada Pension Plan
that this view did not get a great deal of support in the committee, and while I am not suggesting that it should be acted upon now,
I am of the opinion that this question should be studied very carefully in the near future.
I just wish to throw this out to the government for consideration at some time in the * near future. My thought is that pensions should increase as age increases. There is a clause in the present part IV for escalation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak on this point of order before the hon. member continues. As the hon. member suggested, the purpose of the amended rule was to prevent two consecutive general debates. Previously during consideration of a bill an extended debate has taken place on second reading, and consideration of the general principles immediately following, in some cases, led to an extended debate on clause 1. Perhaps I may be allowed to speak to this point of order, Mr. Chairman. Your Honour was quite right in drawing our attention to the amended rule adopted earlier in this session. However, the circumstances leading up to that action are somewhat different from the circumstances surrounding our consideration of this bill.
We dealt with this bill rather quickly last November, commencing our consideration at that time late on a Monday, continuing throughout Tuesday and Wednesday and then

referring it to a committee. At that time we could quite sensibly have extended our consideration of the bill because of the magnitude and importance of it; however, we were quite reasonable at that time in consenting to the suggestion that the bill be sent to a committee for study. That study has been carried out and the bill is now again before us for consideration. At this time, we should be completely free to comment generally on the contents of the bill and the changes proposed by that committee. From my experience in matters of this kind I am led to believe that this bill will be processed more rapidly at this stage as a result of this freedom of comment than could be the case if a strict application is made of the amended rule.
I appreciate the fact that the chairman was justified in drawing our attention to this rule, but I am sure this is an occasion on which hon. members will agree to allowing the chairman to turn a blind eye, at least temporarily, to the rule.

Mr. Chairman, I was about to point out one shortcoming of this proposed measure. I believe that consideration should be given to the suggestion that the pension should increase as the age of the recipient increases. While the bill does contain an acceleration clause, a suggestion was made to the committee studying this bill that a reasonable figure in respect of acceleration would be $3 per month per year.
I understand there are two reasons behind this suggestion. As individuals become older their retiring benefits lessen in value. Their savings also decrease as a result of being used for doctors' bills and hospitalization, or in other ways.
At the present time I am not proposing that the government amend this bill in such a way as to adopt that suggestion, but I do feel that the government should give some future consideration to it.

Mr. Chairman, I am not in a position to provide the minister with figures of that kind. I am not at this time suggesting any specific amount in relation to accelerated pensions, but merely suggesting that evidence of this kind was presented

to the committee, suggesting an amount of $3 per month per year, to be adjusted perhaps every five years. I urge the government to give some consideration to that evidence. If the minister had been in attendance at the meetings of that committee he would be aware that this suggestion was presented on the first day of its sittings. I questioned many other witnesses about this proposal and, although I did not receive the most favourable response possible, I was left with the impression that they also felt something should be done along this line, though perhaps not in conjunction with the bill now before us. Such a proposal would require a great deal of study before it could be accepted.
I should now like to mention briefly some of the areas of this bill in respect of which I feel there are shortcomings. First of all, there is nothing in the bill for those now retired. There is nothing in the bill for those between
65	and 70 who do not receive old age security. Most serious of all in my estimation is the fact that there is nothing for those in the low income earning bracket. Certainly there is nothing for those earning less than $600 and, if self-employed, less than $800. There is nothing in the bill for these people. I have been given to understand there are a great many farmers or self-employed people in eastern Canada who will fall into this bracket, and we sincerely believe that something should be done for this group of people.
I would point out that on Thursday, October 15, a brief was presented by the province of Nova Scotia to the Senate committee on aging. I am not going to read from the brief, but they point out that there are a great many people in that area who will not receive one penny from this bill. These are the people about whom I am concerned.
Evidence in this regard was given to the committee and those who produced the evidence asked that their figures be verified or denied. I do not think there has been any denial. Their evidence was to the effect that of all those retired by 1976, 11 years hence,
66	per cent will receive absolutely nothing from this legislation, 32 per cent will receive an average of $45 a month and 1.5 per cent will receive $119, which amount is over and above the $104.17 static rate because of escalation.
I claim that the bill does nothing for close to two million people in this country and I would refer to an editorial in the Globe and Mail of February 19, 1965 in which it is estimated that something like 2| million people will receive nothing under the bill. What we

I want to refer to students, those who are trying to remain in institutions of higher learning and educate themselves in order to meet the competition of the world in which we live today. We are concerned about the dropout period for these students. There are maybe only 5,000 people who are employed by foreign governments in Canada, but at the moment they are excluded from the bill. We also believe that the penalties provided are arduous. The plan is supposed to be one under which an individual will receive a retirement pension based on 25 per cent of earnings. We believe that the present penalties are too harsh and we will suggest a modification.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say at the outset that I appreciate, as I am sure the committee as a whole does, the dilemma that faces you in the chair on clause 2 of this bill. I am inclined not only to agree with your interpretation but to wish that it might be implemented, and that we might get on with the various clauses of the bill. I also know that there is some point to the argument made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in that if you try to cut off the debate too much we will get into procedural arguments and probably make less headway than we might make otherwise. I suggest as a compromise that we who speak on the first
[Mr. Monteith.l
round try to make our remarks brief. I will certainly do my best toward that end. I would suggest that we not have too many of these general statements, but that we try by general agreement to get on with the clauses as quickly as we can, for after all it is in the handling of the various clauses that we can deal with the points that were raised by the hon. member for Perth, and other points, as they arise.
Briefly, I should like to join with the hon. member for Perth, and with others who I know will follow me, in saying that it was an excellent committee on which we had the privilege of serving in December, and during the Christmas recess that most of the members enjoyed in their constituencies. I have seldom been on a committee that worked as hard as this one did. The attendance was tremendous and members read the briefs and did their homework. The delegations, whatever their points of view, were very helpful and I think our discussions of the bill itself were most useful and that we came up with a number of very constructive suggestions. Some of these suggestions were accepted by the committee. Some of the better ones that I made have yet to be accepted, but at least we are moving in the right direction.
I know that all members of the committee would want our thanks to be expressed to the delegations that appeared before us, and also to our own committee staff and others who assisted us while we were in session, but in particular to the civil servants of the many departments of government who sat with us by the hour and helped us understand the bill and enabled us to suggest some improvements on the basis of our understanding of it. If therefore we have a reasonably good bill before us, credit has to be given in many places, in particular to the very capable civil servants from many departments who worked with us.
I had a letter a few days ago from a person who does not like the bill. In it he complained that any attempt to rush the bill through would be akin to a slap in the face to those who had worked hard to produce reasoned criticism of it. I did not deny my correspondent's right to that view, but I wrote and told him that there was another side to the story, that not only are there some critics who have tried to work out criticisms of the bill but that many hours, many days, many weeks, many months had been spent in producing it, and that we would be engaging in irresponsibility if we did not see

this piece of legislation through, rather than dropping it because there is some opposition to it.
We in the New Democratic party think there are some shortcomings in Bill No. C-136. We think that there are some shortcomings in the total package for security in old age that is before us, in a combination of the Canada pension plan and a revision of the Old Age Security Act. We will deal with those shortcomings as we go along.
I must say in all fairness that most of the shortcomings, in our view, relate to the failure to make adequate improvements in the Old Age Security Act. We think that the Canada pension plan proper, the new contributory earnings related element, by itself, stood up fairly well to the criticisms that were made by the delegations that appeared before the committee. There are flaws even in it, and we have corrected some of them by the amendments we moved and by the proposed amendments we have offered in paragraph 8 of our report. Like the hon. member for Perth, I would be interested in knowing as early as possible how many of our recommendations the government is going to accept.
As I say, in the main we feel that the contributory earnings related Canada pension plan has stood up fairly well to the criticisms that were made of it, and that if the house will make the improvements that we suggested, it will be doing a good job. There are those gaps to which the hon. member for Perth referred, as well as some others. Notably there is the fact that although we are doing something to improve the amount of pension people in the future will have when they pass 65 or 70 years, we are doing nothing now to improve the pension position of those who are today 70 years of age, and over. Until the Prime Minister made his announcement last Wednesday, we were doing nothing to improve the pension position of most of those between the ages of 65 and 70. The Prime Minister's announcement of last Wednesday alters that picture, and it was a most welcome announcement. We are going to improve the position of the people in that bracket. However we are going to take five years to complete the process.
Our feeling, as a party, is that what most of all needs to be done to round out the package and make it a good pension program for the Canadian people, is to raise the amount of the pension under the Old Age Security Act to $100 a month and to make it available at age 65. We will come to this when we reach the details, but I want to make the point
Canada Pension Plan
that our approach to this is different from the approach suggested by the Progressive Conservatives. I do not think I am doing them an unfairness when I say they want $25 additional to be given the recipients of old age security but they want that paid out of the Canada pension plan fund. They have certain other details they will lay before the committee when we get to that part of the discussion. Our position is different. We want the old age security pension itself increased. We want this, not just because we think we must now do something for people 70 and over, for people between 65 and 70, but because we also feel that it will make a better balanced package if the flat rate benefit is that much higher.
As I have said, we will suggest some changes in the Canada pension plan itself. We are still unhappy about the regressive feature of the taxation being imposed by this bill. It is removed to a considerable extent by the $600 exemption, but it is still regressive in that those people with incomes below $5,000 will be paying, instead of everybody paying on all their income. We are still unhappy about people in the lower income bracket having to pay a portion of this contribution into the building up of a fund to be lent to the provinces for investment purposes. There are things like that about which we will talk as we go along. In the main, as I say, we regard the Canada pension plan proper as a good piece of legislation. We feel it is desirable to get it enacted as early as possible and to get it on the statute books.
Along with our acceptance of the Canada pension plan, improved as we shall suggest, we urge very strongly that the government not just think of us as voices crying in the wilderness, but pay attention to our insistence that at the time the Canada pension plan comes into effect, particularly when its benefits start to flow, we simply must be doing something for the people already over 70; we simply must be doing something more than is now proposed for the people between 65 and 70. I say to the government in this house, as I said to the government members in the committee, you simply will not get away in Canada with this piece of legislation if you do not complete the job.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I said at the start I thought we should try to make our initial statements brief; that we should not reveal all our arguments at this point. I shall therefore heed my own advice. I think that in these few words I have indicated the general view of our party. We have waited a long while

Canada Pension Plan
for this kind of legislation. Several years ago our party proposed this two stage type of program, a flat rate benefit and an earnings related benefit. We want them integrated. We want them built in such a way that people will get as high a percentage of their working income as possible, so that the people in the lower brackets will get close to 100 per cent or even more than 100 per cent of their income during their working years. This is our position.
We support two things. We support the Canada pension plan proper, almost as it is. We support the idea of the two programs being put together. We think it would be a much better plan if the old age security pension itself were increased to $100 per month and made available at age 65. This is the aim for which we will be working the hardest as we go through the bill. I hope I have not transgressed on what I suggested might be the ambit of general remarks to be made at this stage. The committee of course will hear from us as we move along.

In keeping with the suggestion that we probably should not go into a wide ranging discussion of all the clauses of Bill No. C-136 I, too, intend to be very brief. I feel there is some validity in the argument that this is the first opportunity members of this house have had to discuss this subject since the bill came back from the standing committee, and that it would be in order for perhaps one member from each party to advance some of the opinions of that party at this time.
First, on behalf of this party, I want to express our appreciation to the members of the joint committee for the long hours they worked during the recess listening to the various people and organizations from across the country who wanted to make their views known in respect of this bill. I feel that we, in common with the other members of this house, owe a great debt of appreciation to the committee. As a matter of fact, the member from our party who was on that committee, and who attended most of the meetings, was the hon. member for Cariboo. Unfortunately he is unable to be here today. If he had been, he would have been making these remarks.
At the outset I want to say that, in so far as we in this party are concerned, we believe that the Old Age Security Act and the Canada pension plan envisaged in Bill No. C-136, should be considered separately. We agree with the principle that there ought to be

introduced in Canada a national contributory pension plan, and that the potential benefits built up should be related to the contributions made. This is in keeping with the position we have taken for a number of years that there ought to be a pension plan available to Canadians that is portable and that is universally available to all Canadians. This, in our view, should not be confused with the right that has been established in Canada, that Canadians reaching a certain age will have some pension available to them such as we have now, under the Old Age Security Act. We realize that in years to come, as the cost of living increases it will be necessary to change and amend the Old Age Security Act in order to take care of those people who now have passed their 65th year, and to take care of those now aged 55 to 65, because they too will be unable to make the contributions necessary to gain a full pension under the Canada pension plan.
Without going into a lot of detail I merely point out that we think we have not reached the end in so far as making adjustments and amendments to the Old Age Security Act is concerned.
There are still a couple of weaknesses in the bill as presented, in spite of the fact that it was amended many times. We believe there should be provision in a national contributory pension plan whereby self-employed people, and others, can undertake to pay a certain amount into the plan over and above the percentage of income set forth in the bill. If the figures now used are actuarially sound there can be no argument about the fact that if a person pays in 1.8 per cent, or 3.6 per cent in the case of the self-employed, he has made his full contribution to the plan, but if such a person wants to pay in more he should be allowed to build up larger potential benefits. In other words we do not agree that contributions should be limited to 3.6 per cent if people wish to pay in more.
The other thing we are most concerned about is that approximately 20 per cent of the workers in Canada will be completely excluded from the opportunity of making contributions to the Canada pension plan. These include casual, seasonal and migratory workers. I can understand the problems involved in keeping track of these people who move from one job to another and whose incomes are not uniform throughout the year. But I do not think there can be any objection made to people in these occupational groups contracting into the pension plan by paying a certain amount into it, and I believe the

potential benefits built up from their contributions should be equal to the benefits that will accrue to people on a uniform wage or salary.
Conversely, if the figures now used with respect to potential benefits are not actuarially sound, and in the event that some subsidy will be required from the federal treasury, then it must be accepted that each Canadian citizen is equally entitled to the same subsidy paid into the fund to keep it going.
There has been a lot of discussion about what will be done with the fund that will be built up, and about some of the problems that may arise from having such a large investment fund built up over the years. We do not accept the argument that such a fund will cause any hardship for private industry in obtaining its capital requirements.
If the fund is going to be made available to the provinces, then to the extent that it is made available for their capital requirements and those of their municipalities, they will be able to withdraw from the private money market and private industry will have that much less competition in seeking its longterm capital. In fact there will be that much more investment capital available to both the private and public sectors as a result of this fund being accumulated.
Further, we take the position that it may be well for Canada to have some of her social capital requirements met out of the universal contributory pension plan fund rather than having the provinces and municipalities go to the private money market to borrow all their long term capital requirements.
With these few brief remarks, Mr Chairman, we generally endorse the provisions of Bill No. C-136. There are some other weaknesses in it which we will discuss as we reach various clauses. We think some amendments may be necessary during the months and years to come, as a result of the experience gained in administering the plan, but we hope we can get this bill passed into law as soon as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few words to say about clause 2 of Bill No. C-136. I really thought we would be allowed to express our opinion during the discussion of clause 1, but in view of your earlier ruling, we shall follow your suggestion and restrict ourselves to clause 2, while referring to two specific points.
First of all, it is a known fact that our group and the people in Quebec are not particularly and directly interested in the
Canada Pension Plan
Canada pension plan, since the province of Quebec will have its own pension plan. However, Mr. Chairman, it must be realized that the two plans are quite different.
We now have the old age pension of $75 a month at 70 years of age, which those who are now 65 years old will get in five years. The two plans should not be confused, as some hon. members seemed to have done a moment ago.
The old age insurance plan should be considered independently from the others.
On the other hand, an increase in old age pension is desirable, we think, if we are really to have a piece of legislation favouring Canadian citizens and not what I would call a Canadian "barbotte". If we propose to help every citizen, from the one who has no income to the one who earns $20,000 a year, we must have a pension plan whereby, sooner or later-and I hope it is sooner than later- the pension would be set at $100 a month payable at 60 years of age.
Then we would be in a position to help and protect fully our senior citizens across Canada and in each of the provinces.
We are in favour of this particular old age pension plan, but we do not accept the pension plan in its present form.
I see that section 2 mentions "applicants". Therefore this plan does not leave one absolutely free. It is really a plan being added to the original old age pension plan which we already have. Let us not impose on one class of workers a burden they do not deserve.
Those who receive from $500 to $5,000 or $6,000, I do not know exactly, will contribute under the plan. I find this plan too restrictive. Once again, it is the pockets of the average worker that are being picked to obtain the amounts needed by the treasury, amounts which could easily be obtained elsewhere. But no, once again money is being obtained from the worker, who is called upon to make sacrifices beyond his powers. Every attempt is being made in Canada to exempt the big corporations and trusts with the largest income in the country and make the small workers supply the money needed by the government for investment in other fields.
Mr. Chairman, the alleged purpose, which I call the fictitious purpose of the government, is to provide a pension for workers at the age of 70. But that is only a smokescreen. The real purpose-be honest with the people, spell it out-the ultimate purpose of the government is to have in ten years $8 billion available for investment in other fields. Where will they get those $8 billion? Not where

Canada Pension Plan
they are at this time, although it would be very easy to get them from our natural resources, from the big companies, from the taxation of foreign capital, particularly American capital which amounts to some 80 per cent. That is not where that money will come from, but from the pockets of the workers as if that class of people had to be maintained at such a low level that they could not raise their voices to speak about their misery.
It is for that reason, Mr. Chairman, that we take very strong exception to this so-called scheme to assist workers, to this sham scheme whose purpose, we are told, is to assist persons at the age of 70, while in fact, the intent is once again to come to the rescue of big interests and give a new push to those who come here to take over all our natural resources and the best part of our income.
We had many reports to read because this is the sixth report presented to us. Some 50 years ago, there would have been only one report because the people were not informed but today, the people are informed, they can see things as they are and they know that once again they will be the scapegoat in this matter. The people know that.
The people should be free to contribute to that plan, so that those who want to get coverage from a secondary plan may do so; we have no objection to that. But let us not make it compulsory with a new tax of 1.8 per cent, which within three or four years will have reached 5 per cent-we know the government-for the average worker. It is a second tax which the taxpayers are required to pay; the income tax is enough and the middle class people cannot afford to pay any more. It is not an insurance premium but rather a tax imposed on the average taxpayer.
That is why we object to this bill. I hope that we shall have an opportunity, when we discuss clause 1, to explain the real reason for our objection, to reveal the government's hypocrisy, for once more the middle class is being subject to taxation. That is the type of hypocrisy the two old line parties have always resorted to in an effort to impoverish the worker in order to control him better.
I will say no more, Mr. Chairman. However, you can be sure that even though this plan does not directly concern the province of Quebec, we know that a similar sham scheme will be introduced in our legislature and we insist on expressing the views of the workers. An end must be put to this bragging of governments and to those smokescreens which cover the underhanded schemes of

financiers who seek to get richer in order to better control the people.
That is why I say once again, Mr. Chairman, that we will vote against this bill.

Perhaps I might rise on a point of order. It has to do with the rule which was adopted on October 9 last and which has been in effect for the latter part of this session. After listening to the remarks which have been made in the debate so far by the leaders of each party, it appears to me they have been concerned, in the main, with possible amendments to the Old Age Security Act. I would point out that it has been made known to them-though this may not be on the record-that this subject will be dealt with at the time part IV of the bill comes before the committee.
It occurs to me that this might well be a suitable opportunity to inform the committee of the proposals the government has in mind for dealing with the amendments suggested and passed by the parliamentary committee, as well as with certain other amendments which may come up later. The technical amendments, most of which will not change the intention of the bill, but rephrase it, with one exception, were passed, and those appear in Votes and Proceedings of Tuesday, February 16 last as appendix D. These amendments, the first being an amendment to clause 2, having been adopted by the committee, will be moved as a part of the individual clauses as amendments. The other amendments which were suggested in the committee report were not, of course, suggested in the language of amendments, but those which the government is prepared to accept and move will be moved as the individual clauses are reached. It was concluded that this would give an opportunity for better attention to the individual clauses of the plan, would direct debate toward the bill which is before us, now, and would leave for debate the simpler matter of the old age security amendments to be commenced by resolution and followed by individual amendments.
I cannot take the floor without joining in the remarks made on all sides about the way in which the members of this house and of the other place worked, for almost five weeks out of the six of the recess, without regard for their responsibilities in their own constituencies and elsewhere and without regard for much needed rest. Nor can I permit the occasion to pass without making

reference to the great helpfulness of the briefs presented. These were obviously the result of a great deal of work and they allowed a rapid and better understanding by members of that committee of the legislation in hand.
I would also join with the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre respecting the public officials and civil servants who have worked very hard in connection with this legislation for at least the past two years, and who prepared from time to time to speak to the committee at its request.
The amendments then, I should like to tell the committee, will be dealt with in that way, the technical ones being moved from the Chair, and the others being moved by the Minister of National Revenue, who is responsible for a large section of the bill, and by myself, as we proceed along through the clauses. Some suggestions have been raised with respect to figures which might be presented at the time we begin dealing with clause 119 and following, and consideration will be given to obtaining these projections. I hope that when hon. members propose amendments on which they have already settled, as I understand my hon. friends opposite have-I did read in the papers the other day that they said publicly not in the chamber but outside, that they were going to move certain amendments-that they too will have some figures at that time, so that the committee will be able to make comparisons. I am interested to see the different suggestions which are made regarding O.A.S. from various party groupings, but in deference to the rule which was adopted in this house on October 9 last I will reserve my remarks until the O.A.S. comes under review after the C.P.P. may have been dealt with clause by clause.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order raised by the minister, I must say I regret that the minister did not take note
Canada Pension Plan
of the reservations which were put forward a few minutes ago from this side of the house. Let us be reasonable and fair about this matter. The resolution which introduced this bill was brought before the house on November 9. Twelve people participated in the resolution debate. We hurried it along and it was passed on that day. Then on November 16, 17 and 18 we had second reading and 26 members participated at that stage. However, that limited time was arranged through the house leaders in a package deal. We had the redistribution bill to complete. We had this bill to refer to a committee. We had an arrangement for seven days to be spent on the main estimates to wind them up. We had reached the 190th day of a very long session. Having made that arrangement with the understanding that this bill would go to a committee and then come back to the house, all I am suggesting is that we have some freedom of discussion now without any restriction, or any invocation of a rule passed in October. This works both ways. We co-operated with the government on that occasion. All I am asking now is that the government be a bit lenient and not press the chairman to invoke that rule.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was interested in having the rule invoked. He spoke on the resolution stage, on second reading and again today. All I am suggesting is that a bill of this magnitude, consisting of 85 pages, a bill affecting every man, woman and child in the country, a bill which has consumed so much time in committee and on which so many representations have been made, should receive full and adequate debate in the House of Commons. This we could have had last fall on second reading, but we passed up that opportunity for the reasons I have already given. We should not now be denied a chance to make general statements at this stage. I hope the chairman will not press the point raised by the minister.

On the point of order raised by the minister, the minister was echoing perhaps the remarks made by the Chair when this debate started. It is not only the rule of the committee-that is 78(1)-that the Chair has to take into account, but also the standing orders of the house. Standing order 59(1) says that in committee of the whole discussion must be strictly relevant to the matter being discussed. It is for the very purpose of trying to enforce this very im-

Canada Pension Plan
portant standing order that the committee on procedure and organization decided to postpone consideration of clause 1 to ensure that whenever a piece of legislation comes before the committee we will respect standing order 59(1).
If it is the desire of the committee that we have a general discussion on clause 2 it may be that the committee on procedure and organization will want to have clause 2 postponed to the end of the bill so that eventually we will be studying each bill backwards, and the last clause will be the first. The Chair is entirely in the hands of the committee, and if it is the desire of the committee to have a general discussion on clause 2, and eventually another discussion on clause 1, I will abide by the direction which I receive. But unless this direction is given the Chair, as the servant of the committee I have no alternative but to ask all hon. members to abide by the rules.
I recognize at the same time that some leniency and leeway has to be granted, and that has been the case with hon. members who have taken part in the debate up to now. I have no objection to hon. members making introductory statements in their remarks on clause 2; but I am asking for the co-operation of all hon. members to respect the rule of relevancy, and I am sure that when we have completed the study of 124 clauses in this bill during the course of our debate in committee, all hon. members will have had an opportunity to take part extensively in the debate.

Mr. Chairman, I rise with some difficulty at the moment because of the point that has been raised. I spoke earlier on the point of order and I do not intend to repeat my previous comments, except to say this. Clause 2 of this bill is, in my opinion, an omnibus clause. It touches almost everything across the face of the bill, and if the hon. lady thinks at any point that I am out of order I think I can point to something in clause 2 which relates to my remarks. And I have several particular clauses to which I wish to refer.
This is the first opportunity we have had to review the work and the report of the special joint committee. In going back over the two and a half months or so during which the committee sat I wonder whether the work was really justified. I know that the hearings were very good and edifying for hon. members who were fortunate enough to sit on the committee. I think they understand in some measure the complexities of the bill. But even
[The Chairman.]
after those two months of study it is quite obvious that we are still in the dark about a lot of its provisions, particularly the cross references and details of the bill.
The members of the committee gave their time during the recess very faithfully, as has been stated. I think the committee was good for the witnesses because they had the opportunity to get their words into print in the transcript of the committee's proceedings, which amounts to many, many pages.
I think the proceedings of the committee were of assistance to the departmental officials who attended. Their thinking in respect of this measure was tested, and in a number of cases they came up with certain amendments which improved the wording of the bill, and others which changed its effect.
Perhaps I should indicate at this point that all of us who were members of the committee were tremendously impressed by the great amount of work that had been done by the people involved. The three individuals who have done the greatest amount of work are those who now sit before the minister. The committee also received some very excellent assistance from the special assistant, Mr. Osborne. We feel that these people have done a tremendous job in putting this bill together.
Having made those remarks, I must say that in spite of the time we spent studying this bill there has been no change or improvement made to the bill itself as it is now presented to us. This bill is practically the same as the bill submitted to that committee for study. Several small changes have been made but nothing has been done to close the great gaps that were disclosed during the committee hearings. Many of us felt from the beginning, right through the committee hearings, until the final report was presented, that there was very little progress made toward filling the gaps apparent in the bill.
Unfortunately the proceedings of that committee have not yet been printed and hon. members who were in attendance at the final hearing can only work from recollection of the statements that were made, the amendments which were proposed and turned down and the undertakings made on behalf of the government. It is unfortunate that we do not have those reports, and I presume this is in no way the result of shortcomings on the part of the committees branch, which worked very hard to keep the evidence up to date. However, we are working under this very great difficulty at this time.

Some changes were made which I think will improve this legislation. For instance, the dropout period of 10 per cent was increased to 20 per cent, meeting the difficulties facing certain individuals such as teachers and firemen, and will go some distance along the road of assistance to students. There was an improvement made in the provisions concerning late marriages. This aspect of the bill was considered at some length by the committee. There were also a number of drafting improvements made to the bill.
I would suggest that one result of the committee's hearings and recommendations was the announcement made last week by the Prime Minister to the effect that old age pensions, instead of being reduced on a graduated scale, will be reduced in stages to $75 across the board. These things are all helpful and I am sure the bill as it now stands is better than it was. However, as I have stated, no changes of substance have been made.
It will be apparent when we deal with this bill clause by clause that any amendment that is accepted will require consequential amendments to several other clauses of the bill. Therefore, it is rather important that we outline at least to some degree the amendments we propose to make. In that way perhaps certain details will be understood. It is my hope also that the government will outline what it proposes to accept in the way of changes. For example, we made a recommendation to the effect that the provisions of the bill be extended to the armed forces and the mounted police. I do not know whether or not the government will accept that recommendation. We are still left in the dark about various other proposals of a similar nature.
Mr. Chairman, I should like now to enumerate several gaps the committee found in the provisions of this bill. The first gap is in respect of individuals over 70 years of age who will continue at the present pension rate and will not be affected in any way by the Canada pension plan. We feel that as time passes this will make a great difference to that category of individuals over 70 years of age. There is also an apparent gap in the provisions of this bill in respect of the group between the ages of 65 and 70. The Prime Minister's announcement in this regard has gone some distance toward closing that gap, but certain individuals will still not be covered in the next four or five years.
There are no provisions in respect of persons who have very small incomes, commonly referred to as the marginal group.
Canada Pension Plan
No provision is made for individuals whose earnings are not discernible because they do not pay income tax or keep accurate account of their expenses, and therefore do not know exactly what their income is from time to time. There is also a large group of individuals who have acknowledged incomes of less than $600 who will not be covered by the provisions of this bill. The proposals we intend to put forward attempt to close these gaps and make the bill as efficacious as it was supposed to have been at the time we commenced our hearings.
Mr. Chairman, if anyone has any doubt as to the position to which I have just referred, relating to the gaps which must be filled, I think it would be desirable for me to read an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on Saturday.

Canada Pension Plan
gap that exists, but which is partially filled now as a result of the announcement made by the Prime Minister. In so far as I am aware, we have not been given any indication of how the additional cost to the old age security fund will be financed. Will there be an increase in the 3-3-4 formula, or will that not be necessary? One knowledgeable person told me that 30 years from now by far the major part of the payments under the Old Age Security Act will be by way of escalation. I shall try to abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and limit my general remarks to clause 2. It was obvious to me before the joint committee had met for very long that the government was not disposed to consider any major amendments to this proposal. I know many of the government members on the committee were impressed by the evidence given. I want to start off by saying that the white paper which the minister issued on the Canada pension plan indicates that this shall be a contributory pension plan to ensure, as soon as possible and in a fair and practical way, that all Canadians will be able to look forward to retiring in security and with dignity. We wholeheartedly endorse that statement.
Then the Prime Minister, following the federal-provincial conference on September 9, 1963, made a statement to this effect, according to the press, that the purpose of the Canada pension plan is to make it possible for all Canadians to retire in security and with dignity. Again, Mr. Chairman, we wholeheartedly support that statement by the Prime Minister. It became obvious to us, after hearing evidence in the joint committee, that the government proposal does not meet the statements made by the minister and by the Prime Minister. There are large gaps which are not filled by the Canada pension plan. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has said, we propose to fill some of those gaps.
Hon. members opposite will no doubt say that this is an earnings related plan, so that those people who are now retired and who are drawing the old age security pension should not get anything from the Canada

pension plan because they have not contributed to it. This is an earnings related plan and the benefits are related to the contributions made. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Chairman, that in most cases the actual benefits received are only remotely related to the contributions made. For example, a person who has contributed for 10 years and then retires, if he has been at the maximum earning level of $5,000, would have paid into the fund through the employee-employer contributions something like $2,000. Yet the benefit that person receives when he retires at age 65 will be over $18,000; so that there is very little relationship between the contributions and the benefits. Furthermore the government itself provides that in practically all of the supplementary benefits there is a flat payment, in most cases of $25, which of course bears no relationship to the contributions or the earnings. Therefore I say, Mr. Chairman, that the argument that we should not pay anything under the Canada pension plan to those who have not contributed is defeated by the very provisions of the bill itself.
There has been ample evidence presented to the committee that the people who are in greatest need today are those already retired, and particularly those in the older age brackets. These are the people who acquired the greater part of their earnings during the depression and the war years, while their shorter period of earnings was in the postwar period when wage levels increased very rapidly. Therefore these people were less able to provide for their future retirement; and yet under the Canada pension plan this group, a very large group comprising some one million people, get no benefit whatever, while on the other hand another group get very large windfalls or bonuses.
Keeping in mind this last group of people over 70 who receive no benefits, we must realize that there is the other group of people who are in the fortunate position of retiring after contributing for 10 years, and for that particular group the windfall to those at the maximum earnings level, or the unearned income, is $18,000. That is the sum that is represented not by what was contributed by the employee and his employer, but a benefit which he did not pay for, and yet those other people over 70 get nothing.
Therefore I sincerely hope the government will consider this because it is obvious, with the fund building up to some $8.5 billion by 1975, there is going to be great pressure by this large group of people to get some benefit

out of the plan. The unemployment insurance fund is an example of how this happens. Obviously until such time as these inequities are remedied the Canada pension plan will become a political football in every election from now on, because these people who do not benefit will say, "Here is a fund built up to $8.5 billion. Why can't some of this money be given to us"? I am saying that we should take the Canada pension plan out of politics and, by making these improvements-

Again I hope the government will consider our amendments whereby these people who would not benefit under the Canada pension plan because of consistently low earnings and also because of chronic unemployment and illness, could be brought under the plan. There is no question but that, once these people find out they will not benefit from the plan, great pressure will be put on politicians to have some of this benefit extended to them.
Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, there seems to be an impression among the people of Canada generally that this plan is good in all respects. They have swallowed part of the propaganda put out by the other side,

that this is something that seems to come directly from above and therefore benefits everybody. I addressed an old age pensioners group in my area and I was amazed to find they actually thought they were getting a benefit under the Canada pension plan.
