We do not yet know what amendments the government intends to present. I hope there are many, and the indications we have had are that this is so. I hope they will not only correct the many minor faults suggested in the various submissions to the committee, but I hope that the amendments which will be presented will also deal with the major faults.
The Canada pension plan as it is detailed in Bill No. C-136, with its various definitions and interpretations set out in clause 2 of the bill which we are now discussing, is a very complicated attempt to set up a national pensions act. We have been told again and again most emphatically by the Minister of National Health and Welfare that its purpose is to enable Canadians to retire in security and with dignity, and certainly we all agree with that. Unfortunately it seems to me that the details as set out in this brute of a bill indicate that this plan will hardly perform as one would hope. In my view, all Canadians will not retire with sufficient pension; many will be omitted entirely from the provisions of the bill.
Many of us are much disturbed by the lofty expectations which this bill has aroused. Consequently, I should like to review very briefly what the bill does, and then outline what the bill does not do, hoping that the bad omissions and faults in it which have not been corrected by the special committee will be largely corrected by this committee. Although the Conservative members of the committee struggled to make suitable recommendations which could correct the major faults in the proposals made in the committee report, at the conclusion of the hearings I made the following statement:
May I state our position. We consider that the rejection of our suggestions leaves the Canada

Canada Pension Plan
pension plan with serious omissions. Nevertheless we support the principle of the plan and intend to vote in favour of the report in spite of its inadequacies. We make this statement because we wish to maintain our right to criticize these inadequacies when the bill is before the house.
And indeed, Mr. Chairman, this is what we hope to do. I have not changed my view that in essence it is a good bill, but there are inadequacies that do require improvement.
The bill, as everyone knows, sets out to collect from all employed Canadians 1.8 per cent of their earnings, the employers matching that 1.8 per cent, while the self-employed such as farmers, fishermen and manufacturers will have to pay the full 3.6 per cent out of their net earnings. One would suppose, under those circumstances, that everyone would be covered by the plan, but this is not so. For there are many who will never contribute and there are many others who will contribute at such a low rate that it is doubtful they will ever receive any very substantial benefits from this plan.
The first earnings related pensioners will be receiving their pensions in January of 1967. That year pensions will be paid to those who are aged 68, 69 or 70 and over. But these people-and this is something that is often forgotten-will be eligible for only one tenth of the full pension that they or others will be able to draw in the later years. To draw this benefit a pensioner must have been making the maximum contribution for ten years, and he must have made it on an income of $5,000 or better.
If I may put it another way, if his average monthly wage is $416.67 or higher he will draw $10.41 monthly from the plan in 1967 if he becomes superannuated at that time. A newly retiring pensioner in 1968 could draw $20.83. This process continues until finally in 1976, when the pension plan matures, a pensioner could get the full rate of $104.17. But remember, this is for those at maximum contributory rates and drawing maximum benefits allowed.
If we consider the case of the pensioner who had a $100 average monthly salary for his contributory years we find that if he retired in 1967 he would only draw $2.50 monthly. This rate would continue upwards until by 1976 he would draw $25 per month. It seems to me that few Canadians realize how low the benefits are, and the press- probably because few of them actually know what the bill does, because indeed it is com-[Mr. Cantelon.l
plicated-have not circulated the preceding facts.
Once a pensioner begins drawing his pension his rate remains at the amount set. However, all pensions once set may be improved somewhat by multiplying by the cost of living index, provided the cost of living index rises sufficiently.
In 1967 contributors may retire at age 68, in 1968 at age 67, in 1969 at age 66, and in 1970 or later at the age of 65. However, a pensioner is allowed to receive an old age security pension at the above retirement ages.
1	think that represents a very worth-while change, as announced by the Prime Minister on Tuesday last. The $75 monthly payment would be added to the payment which will be provided through the Canada pension plan, but in order to receive these payments the pensioner must be retired. If he receives casual earnings between the ages of 65 and 70 a reduction factor is applied to his Canada pension payment and an income tax penalty is applied to his old age security payments.

In addition to these general conditions which apply to everyone, the bill also makes provision for disability pensions, for survivor benefits, for orphan benefits and a death benefit. This again relates to clause 2(1), paragraph (e). The disability pension may be

drawn before age 65 on proof of disability. A flat $25 is paid and a maximum of 75 per cent of the retirement earnings or a total of $103. Children of the disabled contributor will receive the same benefits as those paid for orphans. Survivors' benefits are paid for widows if the contributor had paid for at least two years and for one third of his working years. Orphans' benefits are paid to children who are still at school up to age 18. They are ordinarily paid on the death of the father, but may be paid on the death of the mother, if the mother was the main support of the family.
A new amendment proposed in the report provides for a payment of $25 per month per child for the first four children and $12.50 for each child thereafter. The death benefits may amount to as much as $500. These are good provisions, but it is too bad that again the government does not truly consider this measure as social legislation. If it did, these benefits would start not later than January, 1967, instead of being deferred for widows for two years, for orphans for two years and in disability cases for five years.
What does this bill not do? First, and certainly most important, it deceives the Canadian people into thinking that they will have an adequate pension plan. It misses badly on two counts. First, a large number of Canadians will never derive any benefit from the plan as it is constituted today because they will not earn enough to be recorded. Their pensions are going to come solely from old age security legislation. It is a most regrettable fact that many hundreds of thousands of Canadians earn at such a low rate that they may never be contributors, and hence never draw a cent from the plan as presently constituted. Then there are many millions of earning Canadians who earn enough to be recorded but who are going to find that a 25 per cent of average earnings pension will be extremely low.
For example, we have seen how very low the pension will be for those whose average earning rate has been $100 a month-in 1967 $2.50 a month, rising to $25 a month in 1976. The fellow who retires in 1967 should be forgiven if he feels bitter about what this much advertised universal pension plan does for him. If it were not for the Old Age Security Act he would be in desperate condition indeed with his $2.50 per month for life.
Those already retired are not going to be happy about a plan which does nothing for them. It does give them small increases through the multiplication of their pensions 20220-73ii
Canada Pension Plan
periodically by a cost of living index. The full increase if given would be $1.50 a month, and the first such increase would not be payable until 1968-some raise, and quite some wait.
The senior citizens advancement committee emphasizes a more serious complaint about this fixed amount and cost of living factor. I quote from their submission to the special joint committee on the Canada pension plan:
Price increases constitute a direct cut in pension benefits, reducing all incomes, especially of those living on private, small pensions. Cost of living bonuses limited to two points annually cannot compensate for price rises.
In our opinion, the cost of living bonus as proposed tends to freeze the federal old age pension at $75 a month at age 70.
I might interject that at that time the government had not made its announcement that the $75 old age security would be paid by progressively reducing the age from 70 to 65 years.
We strongly object to this provision and urge that it be struck out. We believe that the federal old age pension and the new pension plan must be adjusted upwards as the national wealth increases, at regularly spaced intervals-something to look forward to-and should be tied to the gross national product and taken out of politics altogether.
I must confess I agree with them that this is one of the worst features of the plan. It is a tacit acceptance of the fact that the old age assistance of $75 is sufficient pension for those already retired. This I cannot accept.
Evidence was presented to the pension committee which showed that in 1976-the first year when the plan is fully operative- there will be 1,880,000 Canadians who will be retired at the age of 65 or over. Of these nearly two million Canadians, 1.5 per cent will be drawing the by then increased benefits of $119 a month, and 32 per cent will be drawing average benefits of $45 a month. This figure was arrived at before we heard the change which the Prime Minister announced, and I expect it will now be somewhat more, but unfortunately I have not been able to calculate that. What will the remaining 66 per cent be getting? The 1,250,000 left will be getting exactly nothing from the Canada pension plan. In other words, two thirds of all Canadians retired in 1976, 10 years after the plan begins, will be getting no benefits from the plan.
The plan is not universal because it does not include people whose incomes are less than $600, or $800 if self-employed. It is not universal because it will not include the un-

Canada Pension Plan
employed. It is not universal because it will not do anything for persons who are now aged, widowed or disabled.
A good national pension plan should be based on social justice. Obviously it should do the most for those most in need. This plan does just the opposite, in some respects anyway. To quote the Canadian association of social workers in the brief they presented to the Canada pension committee, at page 3 they said:
It does little for those who are on marginal or substandard wages or whose employment is irregular. Despite the steps taken in the plan to reach these groups and to ease them into the benefit stream the end result is totally inadequate. As so frequently happens in social security legislation the poor are left in their poverty and the major benefits accrue to the stronger income groups.
This is a pretty strong statement but I believe it is justified.
Many submissions to the committee pointed out that those who retire in the years just after the plan matures, that is to say, the years 1976-78, will have contributed very little and will draw a pension which will have a value several times what they contributed. If we want to take the worst example, that of a man making maximum contributions and drawing maximum benefits at age 65 in 1976, he will have paid 10 times $79.20, or $792, as will his employer also, into the plan and will have a pension, as pointed out at page 149 of the proceedings of the committee, of the value of $12,295. That is a pretty nice windfall.
I want to point out here that I do not have an inherent objection to this fact. As I said before, this is a social welfare measure and some inequities must be expected, but I do think they should be less blatant. The young people of today should not be expected to pay for gross inequities like this, especially since they could be reasonably reduced if we extended the maturity period.
The proposals of my party are eminently sensible and we believe within the compass of the funds provided, as we hope to show when we propose our main amendments which deal with the financial part of the Canada pension plan. Naturally if these amendments are accepted the funds will not accumulate at as rapid a rate as they would under the present bill's terms. However, are we instituting this scheme primarily to produce capital for the use of the provinces, or are we creating a pension plan for Canadians who need help in old age? The answer is easy. I maintain it is the latter, and that 
purpose should not be subordinated to produce capital for provincial uses.
Thus far all of our provinces have been able to borrow the money they needed at reasonable rates on the money market. My own province, so-called socialistic government or not for 22 years, did very well indeed. I do not think it is the function of the dominion government or of this parliament to overtax the contributors to produce provincial capital. This bill provides for over funding.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association had this to say about the level of the funds produced, and I quote from page 5 of their brief to the committee:
The association takes the position that the Canada pension plan as presently proposed provides for too high a level of advance funding. This will result in accumulation of an unusually large pool of funds which apparently will be diverted for use in provincial and municipal works projects of one kind or another.
The association supports advance funding of private plans because there is no guarantee the employer will continue in business and always earn enough money to pay private pensions out of current earnings. This view does not extend to a pension plan which is underwritten by taxing authorities such as provincial or federal governments. In such cases the need for a high level of advance funding is virtually eliminated or substantially reduced.
However, we have this type of funding, so unless we are to throw out the plan and start over again it looks as if we must live with it. The minister also referred to the Unemployment Insurance Act as far as commercial fishermen are concerned. He told us that under this act no determination was made about fishermen being employees, but merely about their being insured persons. This is not exactly what the Unemployment Insurance Act says. Perhaps I could quote briefly from it so that my contention may be on the record. This is from chapter 50 of the statutes of Canada 1956. Section 29(2) reads as follows- I will only read paragraphs (a) and (b) which are the relevant paragraphs for the sake of
Canada Pension Plan
this argument. Certain regulations may be made-
- (a) including as an insured person any person who is engaged in fishing (hereinafter called "a fisherman"), notwithstanding that such person is not an employee of any other person;
The minister's comments were correct to the extent that no determination was made to the effect that a fisherman was an employee as such; merely that he was an insured person. However, paragraph (b) is revealing. It deals with employers and it says:
(b) including as an employer of a fisherman any person with whom the fisherman enters into contractual or other commercial relationship in respect of his occupation as a fisherman;
Here is a determination by statute that an employer of a person in a fishing company is an employer as far as his relationship to the fisherman is concerned. So while the minister was correct, in one sense, that no decision was made to classify a commercial fisherman as an employee under the act, nevertheless paragraph (b) of section 29(2) does declare that a person can be an employer of a fisherman who is not classified as an employee.
What we seek to propose with respect to the Canada pension plan is that a similar arrangement should exist. We suggest we cannot use legal jargon or legal terms, or twist plain meaning to try to make a commercial fisherman other than what he is-to try to make him into a businessman, to try to determine that he is not a workman working for a particular fishing company. This has been the course followed over the years by the drafters of the workmen's compensation act in British Columbia, and by those who argued against the inclusion of commercial fishermen under the Unemployment Insurance Act a few years ago. Their attitude has been to use semantics or legal jargon to legislate commercial fishermen out of the benefit of the opportunities available under certain statutes and put them at a disadvantage as compared with other workmen in basic industries. It is not so much that the government does not want to include commercial fishermen as employees. It is not so much that the government wishes to put the full load of pension plan contributions on the shoulders of the commercial fishermen, but that it is revealing the government's hand or its intentions with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The minister shakes his head, indicating that that is not so. May I take it, then, that the government does not intend to follow the recommendations of the Gill commission in this regard?

The Unemployment Insurance Act twisted the law, and it was my hon. friend's own party that did it, if what he is saying is twisting the law. But what I submit is the correct state of affairs is this: Because of the nature of the fishing industry both on the east and west coasts, and undoubtedly the inland fisheries as well, a commercial fisherman is a workman who works for wages. But also because of the nature of the industry people in the past have given him a designation which makes him neither an employee nor an employer but which puts him in some middle class. This has been the difficulty which has confronted the commercial fisherman ever since parliaments and legislatures started to enact legislation in connection with the relationship between workmen and companies. That is where the twisting of the situation came about both by parliaments and legislatures which either did not understand the full situation or did not want to understand the situation, but instead wanted to enact legislation which would put the commercial fisherman in a much poorer position vis-a-vis his relationship with other workmen.
That is all we are attempting to do-to put before the minister and the government the full details of what is a commercial fisherman, the problems with which he is confronted, and why he should be considered in the same class as other people who work for wages. Whether you can call him an employee or a workman or something similar really does not matter so long as you are interested in making the determination that a commercial fisherman is a person who works for wages, and as such should be in no different position than the minister himself, that is to say, one who pays a portion of his income, within the maximum limits set out in the bill, toward the Canada pension plan and who likewise has somebody called his employer who pays an equal amount toward the Canada pension plan.
As I have said, because of the similarity between the wording in the bill before us and that in the Unemployment Insurance Act, it naturally follows, to my mind, especially in view of the recommendation of the Gill commission that fishermen be excluded from the

provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, that if the government is taking the position, by using substantially the same language, that it is not willing to recognize commercial fishermen as true workmen working for wages, it seems to me that at some subsequent date they also intend to take them out of the ambit of the Unemployment Insurance Act and to follow up the recommendations of the Gill commission, even though the two are really not comparable.
At some subsequent stage of this bill, if we are able to acquire the technique of draftsmanship and can fit it within the rules of the house, we intend to prepare some sort of amendment in the hope of putting this point across in a formal way. Because we think that if this matter were put clearly before the house in a formal way the house would (1) have the opportunity to support it and (2) would undoubtedly support it. There are members both on the government side of the house and on the opposition side who are thoroughly familiar with the operations of the fishing industry. Some of them were fishermen themselves and they realize perhaps more than others what is involved here. Likewise there are some members on the government side, including, as I understand it, the Minister of Fisheries himself, who have said that for the purposes of the Canada pension plan commercial fishermen should be classified as employees and should only have to pay 1.8 per cent of their wages, in the same way as everyone else who receives wages.
In view of this statement, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that it is not so much that we want to pull them out in the open particularly and expose the way these people think about something, but rather that, in view of these statements, there is a bulk of the membership of the House of Commons who would support an amendment or proposal to classify commercial fishermen in such a way that they pay only their fair share of contributions to the Canada pension plan, in the same way as other people in Canada who work for wages and who will also be contributing to the plan.
I realize that this is not perhaps the stage at which to move an amendment. Although there are references in the definition clause to an employee, an employer, employment, and business, none the less perhaps the definition clause is not the correct place to put forward such an amendment. But when we do reach the relevant stage I or one of my colleagues, perhaps the hon. member for

Comox-Alberni who is also vitally interested in the matter, will be able to present a formal proposal on which a decision can be reached by the committee itself. If we do that and the arguments which are marshalled are sufficiently strong to support such contention, parliament might very well decide that it is appropriate and fair to classify commercial fishermen as workmen.

Mr. Chairman, having listened to the debate this afternoon I am reminded of previous debates of this committee. I am at a loss as to how I should approach the subjects I have in mind, because I do not intend to bring forward a package proposal but instead wish to direct the minister's attention to specific aspects of the application of this measure. I hesitate to bring these things to the minister's attention, but feel I must do so because of something the minister stated previously. In this regard I feel that we should be allowed some leeway during our consideration of clause 2. It was my understanding that we would be allowed to discuss various topics in a general way during our consideration of clause 1, as is the normal situation. However, it seems we are to be limited in our consideration of clause 2 to subjects relevant to that clause.
Mr. Chairman, the minister while speaking about this biil said that our remarks must be related to the specific subjects under consideration. I hope the minister will draw my attention to the fact that I am irrelevant, if and when I wander from the subject under consideration. I intend only to present arguments in respect of certain clauses of this bill which I think should be amended before they can be accepted. I am not suggesting in any way that we on this side of the house are in opposition to this measure, but I do intend to make suggestions in respect of certain improvements that obviously are necessary.
The first point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is related to the self-employed category. Perhaps I am interested in this category for personal and selfish reasons because I have the selfemployed farmers of Canada in mind, but I certainly hasten to state that I include fishermen in this category. In view of the fact that the hon. members for Skeena and Van-couver-Burrard have dealt with this aspect of the pension plan I do not feel it necessary to cover the ground again.
Mr. Chairman, I am specifically interested in the application of this bill, or the lack of it, to farmers, fishermen and small businessmen in Canada. To quote from a pamphlet I have before me, which states that the prime test of any pension plan is its relation to equity. Certain Canadian citizens in Canada will not be included for coverage under this proposed pension plan. Any pension plan which is properly conceived and
[Mr. Basford.l
executed must be related to equity. That being true, Mr. Chairman, why are certain categories of Canadian citizens in Canada not covered by this plan? Through you, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister why individuals who are elderly, disabled, widowed or poor-by "poor" I mean those people who are in the lower 10 per cent earning class in Canada-should be left out of all considerations as far as this plan is concerned? Why should an individual who is an Indian, an Eskimo, or one who makes his living from the land, an orphan or a retarded or handicapped person, or frequently unemployed, be left out of consideration in respect of a Canada pension plan?
I presume, Mr. Chairman, that I am probably wandering from this section of the bill but, as I said earlier, we as legislators in this house are concerned with legislation which may mean a great deal to Canada. I admit quite frankly that a great deal of it does. I support much of what is in the bill but, as I have said, a bill of this kind should contain more equity. This is why I have put forward the reasons that cause me to wonder why the bill is not as equitable as it should be.
I want to bring something else to the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman, in a broad way, and I would appreciate your co-operation and that of the minister concerned. I should like to refer to a paragraph of a brief that was submitted to the committee by way of another plea for some sort of amendment to the bill that will provide the kind of equity I have tried to bring to the attention of the committee. The brief has the following to say with respect to the bill:
It cannot be looked upon merely as a social security measure. The very fact that it has gone through so many versions not only attests to the constitutional problems but serves to emphasize the economic implications involved.
I appreciate very much what the economic implications are. I attended the committee meetings as often as I could and I thought I got some grasp of the situation. If the things I mentioned earlier were incorporated into the bill by way of amendment and benefits were paid from the returns under the bill I maintain, and I think others will agree with me, that the plan would cost less. In other words, it would be very much cheaper to the taxpayers of Canada to do it this way by adding to the present bill and taking the money from the pension plan fund than

it would be to adopt the bill in its present form.
I will only take another moment or two, Mr. Chairman, and I know that someone is going to be very happy about that. I should like to put another quotation on the record:
Some people and active workers for a number of years were concerned at the recent action in the House of Commons in giving second reading unanimously without amendment to the proposed Canada pension plan bill. Many responsible people in this country are very concerned about the possible long range and immediate effects of this proposed piece of legislation. And so on. Mr. Chairman, the house is called upon now to consider in committee one of the most important pieces of legislation which any parliament of Canada will be
Canada Pension Plan
called upon to consider for some time. The national pension plan is very far reaching in its effect and is going to affect every family in Canada. For that reason the house should take its time and devise a plan which, as the hon. member for Lethbridge has just said, contains the utmost possible degree of equity as between citizens of this country.
We are dealing with clause 2, which is the section containing the definitions for purposes of the interpretation of the act. I am very glad that the government house leader and the minister have consented to considerable latitude of debate under this section. The purpose of the pension plan is to enable our senior citizens, disabled persons and others who are barred from earning a living in the normal way to share more equitably in our national production. No party in the house has a monopoly on this purpose. All parties in the house are deeply interested, and over the years party conventions and party caucuses of all parties have dealt extensively with this problem. Now, it has come nearly to fruition. May I repeat that this house should take the time that is necessary to devise the best possible plan.
We have given this bill first and second reading and then it was referred to a special committee of the Senate and House of Commons for consideration. May I point out that it was rushed through the house during second reading. After sitting through all the months that this house sat last year without a break, it was found most desirable to curtail the general debate on second reading in order to get the bill before the special committee that had been promised, so that evidence from individuals as well as corporations across this country could be presented to that committee, thus serving the purpose of enlightening all those who are interested in the legislation. As I have said, the debate on second reading of this bill was curtailed and we got it to the committee.
I am very glad to note the attitude on the part of the government, namely that a free and full discussion of this measure will be permitted. Discussion is needed. We have heard the hon. member representing one of the Vancouver seats and the hon. member for Skeena raise points in connection with the fishermen and the different categories into which the fishermen may fit. These matters need to be threshed out so we know where these different classes of contributors and beneficiaries stand under the scheme.
I have saved a few clippings from some of the newspapers indicating the need for fur-

Canada Pension Plan
ther study of this bill. In an editorial appearing in the Globe and Mail of February 18, 1965, I find this, and I agree wholeheartedly with it:
The special Senate committee which studied the proposed Canada pension plan during the recess has not been very lavish with its recommendations for improvements. It has presented a body of information and some technical amendments, but its major recommendations, while moving in some of the right directions, wear a wishy-washy air.
This irresolution will ensure what was already a virtual certainty, that the plan will be exhaustively examined in the house.
Finance Minister Walter Gordon was talking nonsense at the week end when he suggested to a Toronto audience that failure to whip the pension legislation through parliament would be a calamity and the result of efforts by pressure groups that had been against it from the beginning. The plan is of vital importance to every Canadian. Almost the entire house is in favour of it in principle, and every member has a duty to play his part in seeing that it is the best plan possible within our means. The real calamity would be if they did not.
If it takes time, well, important matters cannot be rushed, and surely on such an issue no government retaining its senses would consider closure.
I am glad to note that the minister and members of the government have taken this attitude toward a free discussion, and therefore avoided any suggestion of closure. I continue quoting from the editorial:
Only parliament can have the final word, and it should be a reasonable compromise of all the viewpoints involved. The federal government may yet have to engage in extensive negotiations with the provinces before this is achieved.
Mr. Gordon cannot obliterate these necessary steps to a sensible pension plan by crying obstruction.
Then, I should like to quote from this editorial which appeared in the London Free Press:
Few measures in Canadian legislative history have been rearranged and altered more than the Canada pension plan. It is to come up for final consideration when parliament resumes.
In spite of the changes which have been made many reservations still come from responsible quarters.
Then, there is another dispatch from the Canadian Press which appeared in the London Free Press of February 11, 1965. It quotes the life underwriters association president, Mr. Etherington, as saying that one of the main faults in the plan is that more than one million Canadians now receiving old age security would never benefit from it. Mr. Etherington said that in order to provide a minimum income for this group, old age security payments should be broadened in scope and increased. Widows, orphans and the disabled should receive payments.

Then, the past president of this association, Mr. Donaldson, said that a mark against the proposed plan is that no one has thoroughly assessed it. He asked why the government had not appointed an impartial, well qualified financial expert to assess the feasibility of the plan. He said that almost everyone had attacked it, but had it been approved by an expert there would probably be little criticism. Mr. Donaldson said that Canada should study the United States social security plan and also try to find out whether we can afford a pension plan. The social security plan in the United States started with payroll deductions of 2 per cent. It now is up to 7 J per cent, will increase to 9 per cent in 1968 and 11 per cent in 1971. Canada proposes to offer greater benefits, but to take in less money. How can we do it when the United States which has had 30 years experience, cannot?
These are very important points which have been raised by other people who are experienced in the financial field and in the insurance field. Certainly this house should take cognizance of these objections and make sure that we avoid any of the pitfalls of which they may warn us. The life underwriters association raises some other criticisms. They say that the plan would provide nothing for today's aged. I quote from their criticisms:
Canadians not employed and those with low earnings would receive nothing.
Benefits would rise with earnings and thus provide the most for those least in need.
The hon. member for Lethbridge dealt on this point as well. I continue to quote:
It would provide the largest bonuses to those with the highest pensionable earnings.
The plan would push costs forward from one generation to another.
Its structure is complicated and would be bound to become unstable.
Pressures to use the fund to fill gaps in the plan's coverage would certainly develop, and if they succeeded the fund would have to be rescued by a tax increase.
The administrative problems would be substantial.
While integration of the old age security and private pension plans would be straightforward, integration of the Canada pension plan and many private plans would be complicated.
The reason behind that is stated to be that pension plans in industry generally are sound actuarially, whereas the national pension plan, which contains social security aspects, to some extent would not be actuarially sound.
The indexing of benefits would be an admission that inflation may not be controllable.

Here again we come to an idea which is somewhat frightening. We cannot admit that inflation is uncontrollable. If we admit it is, then how can we ever hope to sell Canada savings bonds and long term government bonds?
The addition of the plan to the old age security program would result in nearly one half the population having little incentive to supplement their savings privately.
I would not agree with that. I do not think a national pension program would have that effect. Far from discouraging savings, the present old age security program has proven to be an incentive to savings.
The brief said the proposed plan cannot be considered universal when some 2,000,000 Canadians fail to qualify because they are unemployed, earn too little, are in "excepted unemployment," do not receive cash remunerations or are now aged, widowed or disabled.
Again there is a plea that the pension be made to cover everyone.
Dealing with some of the subclauses in clause 2, I wish to make a plea that the entire clause be stood until such time as other clauses are dealt with, and I do this because many of the subclauses deal with other clauses in the bill. For instance, subclause (i) says that the "contributory period" of a contributor "has the meaning assigned by section 49." Subclause (j) says that "contributory salary and wages" of a person for a year "means an amount calculated in accordance with section 11." There may be good reason to amend section 11 but if we adopt clause 2 as it now stands it looks to me as though we could not then deal with clause 11. Subclause (k) states " 'contributory self-employed earnings' of a person for a year means an amount calculated in accordance with section 12." Subclause (m) states " 'disabled' has the meaning assigned by section 43," and subclause (n) says " 'Earnings Index' has the meaning assigned by section 21." If we adopt clause 2 as it stands, will we deprive ourselves of the opportunity of giving further consideration to the other clauses? In my opinion it would be wise to deal with these subclauses later.

Before proceeding to pass clause 2, I have an amendment to propose. Contrary to what the hon. lady has just mentioned about 24 members being on the committee and none proposing any amendments, with respect to commercial fishermen there is a very valid reason why this was so.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard also suggested that in a subsequent clause of the bill there is a provision giving the governor in council authority or power to regulate in some way, and thus bring commercial fishermen within the terms of the Canada pension plan as workmen or employees, and that we should defer our thoughts at this time until we see what the governor in council might or might not do with respect to the powers proposed to be given to him. He said, also, that the government would have to receive and study the submissions of the united fishermen and allied workers as well as submissions by other fishermen and groups of fishermen on the west coast. If this undertaking were given it should perhaps be sufficient for the time being.
I submit, however, that it is not sufficient, and I say this because the Minister of National Revenue made a clear statement just before six o'clock to the effect that the

Canada Pension Plan
government did not intend to make any alterations in this bill so as to change any of the provisions which it presently contains, as far as fishermen are concerned. I took that to indicate it was a matter of policy on the part of the government that the position of commercial fishermen under this bill is to remain unchanged. If that is government policy there is no need for us to plead with the government to receive and study representations, a decision having already been made to the contrary.
It might be well to have these amendments moved, or at least perhaps I should move one of them and indicate that there will be a subsequent amendment. Unfortunately I do not have copies in sufficient numbers to distribute to representatives of all the parties as well as to the Clerk at the table. But there are still a few minutes remaining before ten o'clock and if these amendments were put on record now, the committee would have a chance to study them. Then, when we meet tomorrow it will be possible for hon. members to argue one way or the other as to the merits of the proposals. The two amendments I have in mind refer to paragraphs (o) and (p) which contain the definitions relating to an employee and an employer. I think I should read them so that they may be on record in one place in Hansard. As far as an employee is concerned we propose:
That clause 2 be amended by adding in paragraph "o" of subclause (1) at the end thereof the following:
"and includes any person who is engaged in fishing who, for the purposes of this act, shall be referred to as a fisherman."
I would formally move this amendment, seconded by my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni, so that it may be before the committee.
I wish to mention also the amendment I hope to move subsequently. This involves a change to the definition of "employer" and it would read as follows:
That clause 2 be amended by adding in paragraph (p) of subclause (1) at the end thereof, the following:
"and in relation to fishermen includes any person with whom the fisherman enters into contractual or other commercial relationship in respect of his occupation as a fisherman."
I would point out that the amendment before you, Mr. Chairman, and the proposed amendment to the definition of "employer" are cribbed from the present provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act section 29(2) which was enacted in 1956.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion unduly. I will merely repeat that this is a matter of extreme importance and substance to fishermen on the west coast as was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard who is familiar with the fishing industry out there and knows at first hand the importance of this subject matter to those engaged in the fishing industry. I understand there are other members of the Liberal party who expressed support in the committee for the concept that a fisherman should be classified as an employee within the meaning of this bill, or in any event dealt with in such a way that his contribution would be 1.8 per cent of his earnings-the same as the contribution of any workman in other industries-and that the remaining 1.8 per cent of that total contribution should be contributed by the industry or by the company which employs the fisherman, or which buys the catch.
I wonder if I might at this stage call it ten o'clock?

maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-REPORTED DECISION TO ABANDON PASSENGER AND MAIL SERVICE
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-REPORTED DECISION TO ABANDON PASSENGER AND MAIL SERVICE
speechtext:
The question I asked today concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway and its proposed abandonment of passenger service across this country, and its determination to follow through such a policy, is in my view of great importance to members of parliament and to all Canadians. I think there are a great many members who are receiving representations on this subject day by day.
I would preface my remarks by saying that a national railway, even if it had not received vast governmental assistance in the years gone by-as it has-cannot, in a country whose population is strung out along a narrow belt 4,000 miles long, ever be considered as just an ordinary private company engaged in competitive free enterprise. A national railway in this country must be part of the very holding together of our nation and its operations must, to some extent at least, be directed in consequence of this fact.
We have a situation where the top officials and the president of the railway have been

going around the country saying quite openly and blatantly that which for years they said secretly, namely that they were plotting to get rid of their passenger services and carry only freight.

speechtext: Regardless of the profits of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.

maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-REPORTED DECISION TO ABANDON PASSENGER AND MAIL SERVICE
speechtext:
My constituency of Halifax is only slightly involved. We are concerned with the continued service of a dayliner on the Dominion Atlantic Railway, which is a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway, from the Annapolis valley into Halifax. However, my main concern is a national concern. My attention has been directed to the subject because of the fact that the C.P.R. has served notice on the postal department that on June 23 they are going to abandon their mail contracts on trains 7 and 8 from Montreal to Vancouver and on trains 3 and 4 from Toronto to Sudbury, which is just one more step in drying up the revenue so that they can later on justify the abandonment of the service. This is the sort of program which this railway has been following.
I said earlier that this railway had received substantial governmental assistance over the years, and of course they have. In addition they received a strip of land across the country, some of which has been sold off. They found minerals on some other parts, received subsidies and have built up the vast prosperity of the empire known as the Canadian Pacific Railway on the strength of these governmental gifts. And now, like the son who receives an inheritance from his father on the basis that he is to maintain his mother, and then throws her out into the cold winter night-

maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-REPORTED DECISION TO ABANDON PASSENGER AND MAIL SERVICE
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-REPORTED DECISION TO ABANDON PASSENGER AND MAIL SERVICE
speechtext:
-the C.P.R. would keep only that part of its service for which it is responsible to the Canadian public that it feels like keeping. It wants to cast off its passenger service and other services which are of such great importance to keeping this country of ours tied together.
I say only this, Mr. Speaker, that the C.P.R. does have a duty to Canada, and that we in this parliament on both sides of the house to whatever party we belong have a duty to Canada to see that the Canadian Pacific Railway is not allowed to operate like the pirates they sometimes picture themselves, but rather that we see to it that they fulfil their responsibilities to the Canadian
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion people and are not allowed, despite the fact that they are a privately owned company, to carry on this process of abandonment of contracts and services on such a wholesale basis. I suggest that the minister give full consideration to taking the matter up with the officials of the C.P.R. so as to see to it that at the appropriate time hon. members of this house have an opportunity to delve more deeply into the matter.

The author is Mr. Victor Mackie. He says:
The Canadian Pacific Railway is moving to improve the service on The Dominion for passenger traffic by transferring express and mail to fast merchandise freight trains, a spokesman for the railway said Friday.
Rumours have been flying that the C.P.R. was going to eliminate The Dominion. They have originated, the railway believes, from misinformation over the new plans the company is working out now for The Dominion.
Then the next is in direct quotes:
"These rumours undoubtedly have arisen as a result of our plans to improve the service on The Dominion by transferring head-end traffic (express and mail) from The Dominion to fast merchandise freight trains", the spokesman said from Montreal head offices of the C.P.R.
By transferring the express and mail to fast freight trains this will mean that The Dominion service is not subject to slowdowns and interruptions as has been the case in the past. It should mean faster, more regular trips by The Dominion, on schedule.
The Dominion in the future will carry just passenger traffic as does the other crack C.P.R. train, The Canadian, during much of the year.
There is no doubt that it has been late often recently. I know that, because I wake up to the C.B.C. broadcast which informs us which Air Canada flights are on time and which are not, and which C.N.R. trains are on time and which are not, and today it was announced that The Dominion was going to be eight hours late. I just happened to hear
